Japan’s J-LEO Program and the CIAJ Solicitation

JapanDirect-to-DeviceGovernmentLEO Satellite

A deep dive into MIC’s Japan Low Earth Orbit Satellite Communications Project (J-LEO) and the CIAJ call that awarded it. The program subsidizes up to half the cost of a domestically controlled direct-to-smartphone LEO system, capped at ¥148.0bn over three fiscal years from a ¥150bn FY2025 supplementary allocation, with nationwide service required by end-March 2029. CIAJ’s Mar 30–May 29, 2026 call selected RAST with Rakuten Mobile on Jun 30, 2026; company statements describe ~40–50 AST satellites on Rakuten’s 1.7 GHz spectrum. Covers mandatory conditions, governance, players, and comparisons with IRIS² and Korea’s LEO plans.

Japan’s J-LEO Program and the CIAJ Solicitation

Deep dive: MIC’s “Japan Low Earth Orbit Satellite Communications Project for Ensuring Autonomy” (自律性確保に向けた低軌道衛星インフラ整備事業), the CIAJ call for proposals, the Rakuten AST award, and implications for operators and suppliers | Status as of November 9, 2026

Prepared for Paul. Citations in square brackets are clickable and map to the numbered References. Most primary sources are in Japanese; translations are mine. Items marked [UNVERIFIED] rest on a single non-official source, company statements, or conflicting reports. Japanese fiscal years (FY) run April–March; Reiwa (令和) 8 = 2026.

Name check

  • “JLEO” is officially “J-LEO”: the Japan Low Earth Orbit Satellite Communications Project, in Japanese 自律性確保に向けた低軌道衛星インフラ整備事業 (“LEO satellite infrastructure development project for ensuring autonomy”). It is run by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC), Global Strategy Bureau, Space Communications Policy Division [1,2]. It is a subsidy program for a privately owned constellation, not a government-owned or defense system.
  • The association is CIAJ: 一般社団法人 情報通信ネットワーク産業協会, officially “Communications and Information network Association of Japan” [2,23]. Rakuten’s English release calls it “Japan Communications and Information Network Industry Association (CIAJ)”, which is close to the name Paul used [25]. CIAJ did not run its own RFI. It acted as MIC’s fund-establishing corporation (基金設置法人) and issued the call for the indirect subsidy recipient (間接補助事業者) [2,14].

1. Executive summary

  • What it is. J-LEO pays half the cost of building a LEO constellation that is owned, operated and controlled in Japan. The constellation must connect directly to ordinary smartphones on mobile spectrum (衛星ダイレクト通信, direct-to-device/D2D). Nationwide service must start by end-March 2029 [15,1]. Its stated purpose is to reduce dependence on foreign LEO providers. MIC names Starlink, Amazon Leo and China’s Qianfan, and cites two risks: sudden service suspension by a foreign company’s business decision, and slow response to Japanese needs such as disaster roaming [8].
  • Money. The FY2025 supplementary budget set aside ¥150.0 billion by adding a J-LEO menu to the existing Digital Infrastructure Development Fund [4,5]. The call capped the grant at ¥148.0 billion over three fiscal years, at a maximum 50% subsidy rate on eligible pre-tax costs [15]. The winner therefore has to fund at least the other half. Trade press values the full build at about $2 billion [39,44].
  • The CIAJ solicitation ran Mar 30 – May 29, 2026 (noon JST), with an online briefing on Apr 8, 2026. Applicants had to be a Japanese legal entity with an office in Japan, and only one award was planned [15,14]. Proposals were scored on policy fit (pass/fail), the build plan and service continuity [15].
  • Outcome. On Jun 30, 2026 CIAJ selected RAST株式会社 (Rakuten’s preparatory company) with Rakuten Mobile as joint proposer [20]. CIAJ later posted a grant-decision notice for the same pair; the notice is undated, but its file was created Nov 6, 2026 JST [22]. On Nov 9, 2026 Rakuten and AST SpaceMobile announced the Rakuten AST, Inc. joint venture (Rakuten 51% / AST’s Japanese subsidiary 49%). The JV will receive up to ¥148 billion through CIAJ over about three years. AST will supply the satellites [25].
  • Architecture (per company statements). About 40–50 large AST satellites in a separate, Japan-registered constellation filed with the ITU at 690 km and 43° inclination. It will use Rakuten’s 1.7 GHz mid-band spectrum. The cellular base-station function sits on the ground in Japan [41,43]. [UNVERIFIED: company/press statements; no official technical filing reviewed.]
  • Main risks are AST’s launch cadence and track record (BlueBird 7 was lost on New Glenn in April 2026) [45], Rakuten Mobile’s ability to fund its 50% share (not analyzed here), and the tight 2029 deadline. The selection also leaves Japan’s three largest carriers on Starlink, whose D2D services launched in 2025–26 [28,29,30].

2. Origins and policy basis

  • Economic package (Nov 21, 2025). The Cabinet’s “Strong Economy” package says Japan will support building a LEO constellation operated and managed in Japan, to secure communications autonomy. It lists J-LEO (MIC) among its space measures [6].
  • From budget request to supplementary budget. CNET Japan reports that J-LEO first appeared in MIC’s FY2026 budget request as an unpriced item (事項要求). It was then moved forward into the FY2025 supplementary budget [36]. MIC’s supplementary budget summary lists “promoting autonomous LEO satellite infrastructure” at ¥150.0 billion under “strengthening economic security” [4]. The Ministry of Finance fund list shows ¥150 billion for the Digital Infrastructure Development Fund (J-LEO), with the fund corporation still “undecided” at that point [5].
  • Rationale in MIC’s own words. MIC says Japan currently depends on foreign providers for LEO satcom, which is a major economic-security problem. It wants Japanese-operated infrastructure that gives nationwide coverage with no special equipment, serves as a disaster lifeline, and supports emergency communications in mountains and connectivity on large farms [8]. A July 2026 MIC paper adds that Starlink, Amazon Leo and Qianfan are investing at a scale and with vertical integration Japan cannot match. It sees autonomy in satcom as important for data sovereignty [11].
  • Wider strategy. The draft Japan Growth Strategy (Jun 30, 2026), quoted by MIC, names NTN (non-terrestrial networks) as an area where Japan depends on foreign providers and where autonomy is urgent. It commits to infrastructure building and demand creation for NTN [11]. J-LEO runs alongside the Space Strategy Fund, which aims for about ¥1 trillion over up to 10 years [24]. J-LEO itself sits outside the Space Strategy Fund, and the call bars double funding of the same costs [15].
  • Disaster resilience as the public case. The program’s design centers on free satellite roaming for other carriers’ users in emergencies (see §4.4). Trade press notes that Starlink proved useful after the Noto Peninsula earthquake, but that relying on foreign operators for critical disaster communications was a concern [36].

3. Governance, funding and timeline

3.1 How the money flows

MIC gives a fixed-amount subsidy to the fund corporation (CIAJ). CIAJ then makes an indirect subsidy to the private operator, and an evaluation committee of outside experts reviews and monitors the work [8,15]. MIC (the 主管課, responsible division) sets policy. CIAJ runs the call, the review, payments and project management [15].

3.2 Funding figures

  • ¥150.0 billion: FY2025 supplementary budget for J-LEO [4,5,8].
  • ¥148.0 billion: maximum grant across three fiscal years under the call [15,14]. The sources reviewed do not explain the ¥2.0 billion difference from the ¥150 billion budget.
  • 50% cap on the subsidy rate for eligible pre-tax costs. Payment is normally on settlement, with advance payments possible up to 50% of each eligible cost item [15]. If the full ¥148 billion is drawn at 50%, eligible spend is at least ¥296 billion (my arithmetic). Payload and Telecoms.com put the full program at about $2 billion [39,44].
  • USD equivalents: Reuters (via CNA) gave $912 million at ¥162.33/$ [40]; Rakuten and AST say “approximately $1 billion” [25,27].
  • The overall Digital Infrastructure Development Fund guidelines say grants generally run to Mar 31, 2030, and the fund exists to Mar 31, 2031. Extensions apply to some submarine-cable projects [17]. [UNVERIFIED: these are fund-wide terms; I found no separate end date for J-LEO beyond the project period ending March 2029.]

4. The CIAJ solicitation in detail

4.1 Scope and eligibility

  • What it funds. Part of the cost of the LEO constellation and other facilities needed to make D2D on mobile-phone spectrum available to general users by end-March 2029 [15]. MIC summarizes the eligible items as (1) satellite procurement, (2) launch and (3) ground facilities [8].
  • Eligible cost lines. Satellite purchase, or in-house build parts (bus, power, comms, propulsion, AOCS, thermal, antennas, transceivers, base-station equipment, monitoring and control), plus assembly and test. Also ground facilities (towers, buildings, power, antennas, transceivers, servers and software licenses), land and access roads, and launch services (vehicle, integration, transport, launch insurance, licensing) and in-orbit testing. Excluded: office overheads, executive pay, excessive equipment and post-project O&M [15].
  • Procurement rules. Multiple quotes are required. Profit must be stripped out when buying from oneself, 100%-owned group companies or affiliates [15]. This matters for the AST supply chain, since AST owns 49% of the recipient JV [25].
  • Eligibility. Applicants must be a legal entity under Japanese law with an office in Japan, and have the technical, organizational and financial capacity. Consortia are allowed, but every member must meet the requirements and a lead must be named. Standard anti-organized-crime and debarment checks apply [15]. The web page says “principal office (主たる事業所) in Japan”, while the PDF says “an office” [14,15]. No foreign-ownership limit appears in the documents reviewed: Rakuten AST is 49% foreign-owned [25].
  • Number of awards: one [15]. Applications had to be in Japanese [14].

4.2 Mandatory conditions (the “Must” tests)

Area

Condition (Guidelines §3.1)

Src

Autonomy ①

The recipient must own, operate and manage the LEO infrastructure

[15]

Autonomy ②

All ground facilities for domestic D2D (gateways, SOC, POC, NOC, etc.) must be located in Japan

[15]

Autonomy ③

Spectrum used must go through ITU coordination via MIC (i.e., a Japanese filing)

[15]

Infrastructure ①

D2D service on mobile spectrum to ordinary smartphones nationwide by end-March 2029

[15]

Infrastructure ②

During the project period, video calls possible nationwide for about 70% of each day; afterwards, self-funded build-out to continuous nationwide service

[15]

Infrastructure ③

Support emergency inter-carrier roaming via satellite (full-roaming, excluding emergency calls), per the MIC IP Network Facilities Committee design

[15]

Infrastructure ④

Voice, data and SMS via satellite under emergency roaming must be free of charge to partner and stricken carriers while the funded satellites operate

[15]

Post-build ①

Keep infrastructure at or above the completed level for 5 years

[15]

Post-build ②

Before the period ends, study domestic satellite manufacturing, domestic launch and operations for the next generation, and consult MIC

[15]

Additional services such as satellite IoT are allowed on top of D2D [15]. MIC can change conditions during the project and for five years after it, in consultation with the recipient [15].

4.3 Evaluation

  • Process: document screening (with possible shortlisting), then an applicant presentation, a committee hearing, committee evaluation and the decision. Scores and reasons are not disclosed [15].
  • Criterion 1, policy fit (Must): every autonomy, infrastructure and post-build condition must be met [15].
  • Criterion 2, implementation plan (Want). Infrastructure level: the 2029 start and the 70% video-call target. Technical design: satellite specs, supplier, number, orbit and inclination; ground stations; device coverage; spectrum and licenses; roaming. Operations, supply-chain and security design. Schedule realism: parts lead times, launch vehicle and booking, carrier network changes, handset software, ITU coordination and landing rights. Also risk planning, KPIs, fair pricing, and funding and staffing [15].
  • Criterion 3, service continuity (Want): a path to continuous nationwide service; 5-year P&L, cash-flow and balance-sheet plans; revenue logic including overseas and B2B; a plan for domestic manufacturing, launch and operations [15].
  • Shared factors: top-management commitment, and relevant experience in satcom, large projects and international partnerships [15].

4.4 Deliverables and obligations

  • Application set (forms 1–8): application, proposal (summary, implementation plan, business plan), cost estimate with evidence, financial plan (funding, investment cash flow, P&L, funding sources, staffing), master and detailed schedules, and declarations, plus a consortium agreement [15,14]. Grant application forms 9–11 come after selection [19].
  • Monitoring: weekly reporting on the implementation plan and monthly reporting on the business plan to CIAJ. Quarterly advice from the committee, an annual on-site evaluation and annual interim audits. CIAJ can halt or review the project based on risk and progress [15].
  • Plans required after selection. The implementation plan covers constellation specs, payload, launch, ground stations and satellite control (including who operates it), carrier-network changes, spectrum and licensing, roaming, security, O&M and supply-chain risk. The business plan covers customers, pricing, competition analysis, cost reduction, an overseas expansion scenario, onshoring and staffing [15].
  • After the project: a completion report with KPIs (quality, scale, usage), then operating reports within 30 days of each fiscal year-end for five years. Disposal of funded assets is restricted [15,17].

5. Architecture and technical concept

The program sets outcomes, not a design [15]. What follows is the winning team’s publicly stated concept.

Element

Rakuten AST / AST SpaceMobile concept

Src

Service

D2D broadband (voice, data, video) to unmodified smartphones; satellite IoT for logistics, infrastructure monitoring, construction and agriculture planned

[25,41]

Satellites

Large AST BlueBird-class satellites; next-gen phased array about 223 m², ~2× Block 1 peak speed (Block 1 demonstrated 98.9 Mbps peak downlink)

[25]

Constellation size

Eventually 40–50 satellites [UNVERIFIED: company statement]

[41,43]

Orbit

690 km, 43° inclination per ITU filing, optimized for Japan; separate from AST’s US-licensed 53° constellation [UNVERIFIED: AST COO statement]

[43]

Coverage goal

At least 70% of time nationwide, average 80–85% [UNVERIFIED: AST COO statement]

[43]

Spectrum

1.7 GHz mid-band currently assigned to Rakuten by MIC (J-LEO); 700 MHz low-band for the separate “Rakuten Saikyo Satellite Service”

[43,41]

Ground segment

Cellular base-station equipment on the ground in Japan; satellites act as large relays; software updates and beam steering controlled domestically

[25,43]

Registration

Japan as state of registry; ITU-filed via Japan

[41,15]

Launch

Designed for several launch providers; talks with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries on future launches [UNVERIFIED]

[43,41]

Optical inter-satellite links

Not mentioned in the J-LEO conditions or company materials reviewed

[15]

  • AST re-filed with the ITU before the award. ITmedia reports that AST’s March 2026 ITU filing changed its planned 248-satellite constellation into a 249-satellite design, with 192 satellites at 690 km and 53° plus smaller near-polar, 520 km and 460 km shells. This improves coverage at Japanese latitudes [38]. The J-LEO system is described as a separate 43° constellation [43], so how the two filings relate is [UNVERIFIED].
  • Two Rakuten constellations, not one. The J-LEO system is separate from the Rakuten Saikyo Satellite Service (Rakuten最強衛星サービス), which runs on AST’s US-registered satellites using 700 MHz. That service starts commercial-environment testing within 2026, free of extra charge for now, with only 13 satellites in operation, so coverage is time-limited [42,41].
  • Spectrum discrepancy. Telecoms.com suggests Rakuten’s exclusive 700 MHz holdings tipped the award [44]. Rakuten and Impress say J-LEO uses 1.7 GHz [43,41]. MIC’s 700 MHz D2D technical conditions (Jun 24, 2026) are a separate rule-making [12]. Treat the “700 MHz decided it” claim as [UNVERIFIED].
  • Coverage realism. Before the award, ITmedia argued that meeting the 70% video-call target nationwide would need at least several hundred LEO satellites [37]. Rakuten/AST’s 40–50 figure depends on its much larger antennas [43]. Neither claim has been independently verified, and this is the main technical question to watch.
  • Security and sovereignty rest on ownership, all-domestic ground control, a Japanese ITU filing and supply-chain and security plans that CIAJ must approve [15,17]. No public material specifies encryption, anti-jam or lawful-intercept design.

6.2 Other bidders and Japanese industry

  • Rival bids. Payload reported KDDI–SpaceX and an MDA Space-led consortium as contenders. Telecoms.com says KDDI/Starlink was the strongest rival bid, and MDA Space also took part [39,44]. [UNVERIFIED: CIAJ has not published the list of applicants.]
  • KDDI, SoftBank, NTT Docomo all offer Starlink-based D2D: au Starlink Direct (Apr 10, 2025, the first in Japan), SoftBank Starlink Direct (Apr 10, 2026) and docomo Starlink Direct (from Apr 27, 2026) [28,29,30]. KDDI also supplied Starlink to the SDF for its 2023–24 trial [34].
  • NTT and SKY Perfect JSAT became authorized Amazon Leo resellers in Japan in June 2026 [31,32]. Neither is in J-LEO.
  • Mitsubishi Electric builds MoD’s next GEO defense comsat with an MDA Space digital payload [33]. MHI is reportedly in launch talks with AST [43].
  • Space Compass, NICT, Axelspace and NEC are developing a LEO optical-communications constellation base technology under NEDO [9]. Synspective, iQPS (QPS-SAR) and Axelspace run Earth-observation constellations [9]. None has a stated J-LEO role. [UNVERIFIED: any supplier role for Japanese firms in Rakuten AST has not been announced.]

7. Relationship to Starlink, OneWeb, Amazon Leo and defense

  • Commercial reality today. Japan’s D2D market runs on Starlink across the three largest carriers [28,29,30]. The Cabinet Office counts more than 9,600 Starlink satellites operating, against 177 Amazon Leo and 651 OneWeb (Jan 2026) [9]. J-LEO does not ban foreign services. It funds a domestically controlled alternative for D2D, so Japan will have Starlink D2D and a Japan-registered AST-based system side by side.
  • Defense. J-LEO is a civil MIC program; its mandatory roaming feature is about disasters. Rakuten’s chairman said use for defense is “basically peaceful use” but other possibilities may arise [43]. MoD’s own satcom is separate. Its FY2026 space budget is about ¥174.0 billion in contracts (¥218.3 billion in spending). That includes ¥88.2 billion for next-generation defense comsats, ¥8.7 billion for PATS (Protected Anti-Jam Tactical SATCOM) equipment, and ¥1.1 billion for Starlink equipment on ships [35]. MoD trialed Starlink (via KDDI) from Jan 2023 to Mar 2024, used it in the Noto earthquake response, and contracted SoftBank to trial OneWeb [34].
  • US alliance and Taiwan contingency. No official J-LEO document mentions the US alliance or Taiwan. The rationale is framed as economic security and disaster resilience [8,11]. A sovereign D2D layer could improve continuity for the Nansei islands in a crisis, but that is my inference [UNVERIFIED]. It also still depends on a US satellite supplier (AST) and, so far, US launchers [25,45].

J-LEO is the smallest and fastest of these, and the only one built purely for D2D on handset spectrum rather than broadband or government secure communications. It buys autonomy by controlling the infrastructure, not by building it at home, and it defers domestic manufacturing and launch to a study for the next generation [15].

9. Opportunities and risks for foreign and commercial players

Opportunities

  • Foreign technology is allowed. The rules require Japanese legal entities, ownership and ground control, not Japanese hardware. AST holds 49% of the recipient [15,25]. The template is a foreign constellation supplier plus a Japanese operator JV.
  • Ground segment and integration in Japan. All gateways and SOC, POC and NOC sites must be in Japan, and the funded costs include towers, buildings, power, antennas, servers and software [15]. That creates contracts for Japanese and foreign ground-equipment vendors and integrators.
  • Launch. Launch services and insurance are eligible costs [15], and AST says it uses several providers [43].
  • Roaming and core-network work with the other carriers for free emergency roaming [15].
  • Follow-on generation. The required study of domestic manufacturing and launch before 2029 points to later Japanese content opportunities [15].

Risks

  • Single award. The main J-LEO subsidy is gone for this cycle [15,20]. MIC has not announced any second round [UNVERIFIED].
  • Delivery risk. AST lost BlueBird 7 on New Glenn in April 2026 [45], and pre-award analysis doubted 40–50 satellites could meet the 70% video-call target [37]. Failing the conditions can lead to cancellation and repayment [15].
  • Funding risk. The recipient must fund at least 50%. Rakuten Mobile’s finances were not assessed in this report.
  • Policy and condition drift. MIC can change conditions for up to five years after the project [15].
  • Market risk. Japan’s three largest carriers are on Starlink D2D [28,29,30]. J-LEO business plans must show overseas and B2B revenue [15], and AST intends to sell J-LEO capacity abroad [25].

10. Open questions and what to watch

  • Exact grant amount and schedule of disbursement per fiscal year (only the ¥148bn cap is public) [22,15].
  • Constellation filing details (ITU/MIC), launch contracts (MHI or others) and first launch date for J-LEO satellites [43].
  • Whether KDDI, Docomo and SoftBank sign emergency-roaming agreements with Rakuten AST, and how the MIC IP Network Facilities Committee design is implemented [15].
  • Whether any Japanese suppliers (NEC, Mitsubishi Electric, ground-station integrators) win Rakuten AST work.
  • AST’s Block 2 launch cadence through 2027–28 and in-orbit performance at Japanese latitudes [45,27].
  • How J-LEO relates to MoD’s future LEO satcom needs; no linkage has been announced [35].
  • Whether a second J-LEO round or a follow-on program for domestic satellites is funded (not announced).

Caveats

  • Most primary documents are in Japanese; translations and paraphrases are mine.
  • Constellation size, orbit, coverage and launch details come from Rakuten/AST statements reported on Nov 9–10, 2026, not from regulatory filings.
  • The applicant list, scores, the exact grant amount and the date of the grant decision are not public.
  • The MIC J-LEO results PDF (main_content/001083517.pdf) returned an HTML page to automated download. The same slide is cited from the Cabinet Office copy [10] and MIC’s July 2026 paper [11].
